l: Hiram, The First Book of Kings, Chapter 7
s: Hiram, brought from Tyre by King Solomon, is the son of a widow of the tribe of Naphtali and of a Tyrian father who worked in bronze. He was filled with wisdom, understanding, and skill, and made the two pillars, the molten sea, the ten bases and basins, and the pots, shovels, and basins. He finished all the work he did for Solomon in the LORD's house.

l: house of the LORD (the temple Solomon built), The First Book of Kings, Chapter 7
s: The LORD's house receives the bronze work Hiram made for it, including the pillars at its porch, the sea, the bases, and the basins. Solomon furnishes it with gold items, and the doors of the inner house and the temple have gold hinges. All the work is finished, and the things David dedicated are placed in its treasuries.

l: bronze pillars (Jachin and Boaz), The First Book of Kings, Chapter 7
s: Hiram made two bronze pillars, each eighteen cubits high with a twelve-cubit circumference, topped with molten bronze capitals of five cubits decorated with nets, chain work, pomegranates, and lily work. They were set up at the porch of the temple, the right one named Jachin and the left one named Boaz.

l: molten sea, The First Book of Kings, Chapter 7
s: The molten sea was made ten cubits from brim to brim and five cubits high, with a thirty-cubit circumference, a hand width thick, and a brim like a lily flower, and it held two thousand baths. It stood on twelve oxen facing the four directions, three each, and was placed on the right side of the house eastward toward the south.

l: ten bronze bases, The First Book of Kings, Chapter 7
s: Hiram made ten bronze bases, each four cubits long and wide and three cubits high, with panels showing lions, oxen, and cherubim, four bronze wheels like chariot wheels, and corner supports. All were cast in one casting, one measure, and one form. Each carried a bronze basin of forty baths, and five bases were set on each side of the house.

l: golden vessels and furnishings of the LORD's house, The First Book of Kings, Chapter 7
s: Solomon made the golden altar, the gold table for the show bread, ten lamp stands of pure gold (five on each side before the inner sanctuary), and gold flowers, lamps, and tongs. He also made cups, snuffers, basins, spoons, and fire pans of pure gold, and gold hinges for the doors of the most holy place and the temple.

l: The First Book of Kings, The First Book of Kings, Chapter 8
s: King Solomon gathers Israel's elders and people at Jerusalem in the month Ethanim to bring the ark of the LORD's covenant into the newly built house, where it is placed in the most holy place beneath the cherubim's wings. A cloud fills the house with the LORD's glory so that the priests cannot minister. Solomon blesses the assembly, recounts the LORD's promise to David that his son would build the house, and offers a long prayer asking the LORD to hear Israel, the foreigner, and exiles who pray toward the house, and to forgive them. He then blesses the people, urging them to be wholly committed to the LORD. Solomon and all Israel offer vast sacrifices and hold a fourteen-day feast dedicating the house, after which the people go home joyful.

l: Solomon, The First Book of Kings, Chapter 8
s: Solomon assembles Israel's elders and leaders, brings the ark into the house he built, and blesses the assembly, saying the LORD has fulfilled his word to David. He prays the long dedicatory prayer, blesses the people again, offers enormous sacrifices, and holds the feast before sending the people home.

l: the LORD, The First Book of Kings, Chapter 8
s: The LORD's glory fills the house in a cloud so that the priests cannot stand to minister. He is described as having chosen David and fulfilled his promise that David's son would build the house, and Solomon asks him to hear, forgive, and maintain the cause of Israel and of foreigners who pray toward the house. Solomon says that heaven and the heaven of heavens cannot contain him, and that he alone knows the hearts of all people.

l: Israel, The First Book of Kings, Chapter 8
s: Israel's elders, tribal heads, and all the men assemble at the feast and sacrifice countless sheep and cattle before the ark. Solomon's prayer asks the LORD to forgive them when they sin and repent, and he exhorts them to keep the LORD's commandments. They keep the feast for fourteen days and go home joyful and glad.

l: David, The First Book of Kings, Chapter 8
s: David is recalled as having had it in his heart to build a house for the LORD's name, and the LORD said he did well but that his son would build it instead. Solomon says the LORD has now fulfilled that word, and he asks that the LORD keep his promise that David will not lack a man on Israel's throne.

l: ark of the LORD's covenant, The First Book of Kings, Chapter 8
s: The priests bring the ark, with the Tent of Meeting and its holy vessels, up from David's city, Zion, and place it in the inner sanctuary beneath the cherubim's wings. Its poles are long enough to be seen from the holy place but not outside, and it contains only the two stone tablets Moses put there at Horeb.

l: house of the LORD (the temple Solomon built), The First Book of Kings, Chapter 8
s: The house receives the ark in its most holy place and is filled with a cloud and the LORD's glory. Solomon calls it a house of habitation for the LORD forever, though he acknowledges even heaven cannot contain God, and asks that the LORD's eyes be open toward it night and day. It is dedicated by Solomon and all Israel with sacrifices, and the middle of the court before it is made holy because the bronze altar is too small.

l: Solomon's prayer, The First Book of Kings, Chapter 8
s: Solomon praises the LORD as incomparable and covenant-keeping, then asks him to hear and forgive when people pray toward the house in cases of oath-swearing, defeat, drought, famine, pestilence, war, and exile. He also asks that the LORD answer the foreigner's prayer so all peoples may know his name. It ends with Solomon rising from kneeling and blessing the assembly.

l: dedication feast, The First Book of Kings, Chapter 8
s: Solomon and all Israel, from the entrance of Hamath to the brook of Egypt, hold the feast before the LORD for seven days and seven more, fourteen in all. Solomon offers twenty-two thousand cattle and one hundred twenty thousand sheep as peace offerings, and on the eighth day he sends the people away and they bless him.

l: The First Book of Kings, The First Book of Kings, Chapter 9
s: After Solomon finishes building the LORD's house and the king's house, the LORD appears to him a second time and promises to establish his throne forever if he walks in integrity, but warns that Israel and the temple will be cast out if he or his children serve other gods. After twenty years of building, Solomon gives Hiram king of Tyre twenty Galilean cities in return for cedar, cypress and gold, but Hiram is displeased and calls them the land of Cabul. Solomon conscripts forced labor to build the LORD's house, his own house, Millo, the wall of Jerusalem, Hazor, Megiddo, Gezer and other cities, using the surviving non-Israelite peoples as bondservants while Israelites serve as soldiers and officers. Pharaoh's daughter moves to her own house, and Solomon offers sacrifices three times a year. Solomon also builds a fleet at Ezion Geber, and Hiram's sailors help bring back 420 talents of gold from Ophir.

l: Solomon, The First Book of Kings, Chapter 9
s: Solomon finishes the LORD's house and his own house, and receives a second appearance of the LORD with a conditional promise and warning. He gives Hiram twenty cities, conscripts forced labor for his many building projects, offers sacrifices three times a year, and builds a fleet at Ezion Geber that brings gold from Ophir.

l: the LORD, The First Book of Kings, Chapter 9
s: The LORD appears to Solomon a second time, as at Gibeon, says he has heard his prayer, and declares he has made the house holy to put his name there forever. He promises to establish Solomon's throne if he is faithful and warns he will cut Israel off from the land if Solomon or his children serve other gods.

l: Hiram, The First Book of Kings, Chapter 9
s: Hiram king of Tyre has furnished Solomon with cedar, cypress and gold, and receives twenty cities in Galilee in return. He is displeased with them, calling them Cabul, yet sends Solomon 120 talents of gold and sends experienced sailors with Solomon's servants on the fleet to Ophir.

l: Israel, The First Book of Kings, Chapter 9
s: Israel is warned that if the king or his children abandon the LORD, it will be cut off from the land and become a proverb and a byword among all peoples. Israelites are not made bondservants by Solomon but serve as men of war, servants, princes, captains and chariot and cavalry commanders.

l: house of the LORD (the temple Solomon built), The First Book of Kings, Chapter 9
s: The LORD's house is completed and the LORD declares he has made it holy to put his name there forever, with his eyes and heart perpetually there. He warns that if Israel turns away, he will cast the house out of his sight and it will become an object of astonishment to passersby. Solomon also offers sacrifices on the altar there three times a year.

l: twenty cities in Galilee (Cabul), The First Book of Kings, Chapter 9
s: Solomon gives these twenty cities in the land of Galilee to Hiram after twenty years of building. Hiram visits them, is displeased, and calls them the land of Cabul, a name that remains to this day.

l: forced labor, The First Book of Kings, Chapter 9
s: Solomon conscripts forced labor to build the LORD's house, his own house, Millo, Jerusalem's wall, Hazor, Megiddo and Gezer, along with storage cities and cities for chariots and horsemen. He raises a levy of bondservants from the surviving Amorites, Hittites, Perizzites, Hivites and Jebusites, not from the Israelites, and 550 chief officers oversee the work.

l: God's conditional promise and warning to Solomon, The First Book of Kings, Chapter 9
s: The LORD promises that if Solomon walks in integrity and uprightness as David did and keeps his statutes, his throne over Israel will be established forever. If Solomon or his children turn away to serve other gods, the LORD will cut Israel off from the land and cast out the house, and passersby will say it happened because they abandoned the LORD who brought their fathers out of Egypt.

l: The First Book of Kings, The First Book of Kings, Chapter 10
s: The queen of Sheba, having heard of Solomon's fame, travels to Jerusalem with a great caravan of spices, gold, and precious stones to test him with hard questions. Overwhelmed by his wisdom, house, table, and servants, she praises Solomon and the LORD his God, gives him gold, spices, and gems, and returns home after receiving all she desired. The chapter then details Solomon's immense wealth: 666 talents of gold yearly, golden shields and bucklers, an ivory and gold throne guarded by lions, gold drinking vessels, and the Tarshish fleet bringing gold, silver, ivory, apes, and peacocks. Solomon exceeds all earth's kings in riches and wisdom, receives yearly tribute from those who seek him, and amasses chariots and horsemen, importing horses and chariots from Egypt and exporting them to the Hittite and Syrian kings.

l: Solomon, The First Book of Kings, Chapter 10
s: Solomon answered all the queen of Sheba's hard questions, showed her his house, table, servants, and ascent to the LORD's house, and gave her all she desired besides his royal bounty. He built a great ivory and gold throne, made golden shields and bucklers, and used almug wood for pillars and instruments. He exceeded all earth's kings in riches and wisdom, gathered 1,400 chariots and 12,000 horsemen, and traded horses and chariots from Egypt to the kings of the Hittites and Syria.

l: queen of Sheba, The First Book of Kings, Chapter 10
s: The queen of Sheba came to Jerusalem with a very great caravan to test Solomon with hard questions, and was left with no more spirit in her after seeing all he had. She declared that not even half had been told her, praised the LORD for setting Solomon on the throne, and gave him 120 talents of gold, abundant spices, and precious stones. She received all she desired and returned to her own land with her servants.

l: the LORD, The First Book of Kings, Chapter 10
s: The LORD is blessed by the queen of Sheba, who says he delighted in Solomon and set him on Israel's throne because he loved Israel forever, so that Solomon might do justice and righteousness. His house is where Solomon's ascent leads and for which almug wood pillars were made. God is also said to have put wisdom in Solomon's heart.

l: Solomon's wisdom, The First Book of Kings, Chapter 10
s: Solomon's wisdom drew the queen of Sheba to test him, and he answered every question with nothing hidden from him. She said the reality exceeded the report she had heard, and called his men happy for hearing it. All the earth sought his presence to hear the wisdom God had put in his heart, and he exceeded all kings in wisdom.

l: Solomon's wealth, The First Book of Kings, Chapter 10
s: Solomon's wealth included 666 talents of gold in one year, besides revenue from traders, merchants, kings, and governors, and gifts from the queen of Sheba. He had golden bucklers and shields, an ivory throne overlaid with fine gold, and gold vessels, with silver considered of little value; his Tarshish fleet brought gold, silver, ivory, apes, and peacocks. He received yearly tribute, made silver as common as stones in Jerusalem, and exceeded all earth's kings in riches.

l: The First Book of Kings, The First Book of Kings, Chapter 11
s: King Solomon loved many foreign women, including Pharaoh's daughter, and had seven hundred wives and three hundred concubines who turned his heart to other gods. He built high places for Chemosh and Molech and worshiped Ashtoreth and Milcom, so the LORD announced he would tear the kingdom from Solomon's son, leaving one tribe for David's sake. The LORD raised up adversaries against Solomon: Hadad the Edomite, who had fled to Egypt as a child, and Rezon the son of Eliada, who reigned in Damascus. The prophet Ahijah the Shilonite tore a new garment into twelve pieces and told Jeroboam he would receive ten tribes; Solomon sought to kill Jeroboam, who fled to Shishak in Egypt. Solomon reigned forty years, died, and was succeeded by his son Rehoboam.

l: Solomon, The First Book of Kings, Chapter 11
s: Solomon loved many foreign women, had seven hundred wives and three hundred concubines, and was led by them after other gods in his old age. He built high places for Chemosh and Molech, and his heart was not perfect with the LORD as David's was. He sought to kill Jeroboam, reigned forty years, died, and was buried in David's city, with Rehoboam reigning in his place.

l: the LORD, The First Book of Kings, Chapter 11
s: The LORD was angry at Solomon for turning from him after appearing to him twice, and declared he would tear the kingdom away, sparing it in Solomon's days and leaving one tribe for David's and Jerusalem's sake. He raised up Hadad and Rezon as adversaries, and through Ahijah promised Jeroboam ten tribes and a sure house if he obeyed.

l: David, The First Book of Kings, Chapter 11
s: David is the standard of a wholehearted heart against which Solomon is judged. For his sake the LORD delays the kingdom's tearing until Solomon's son's time and leaves one tribe so that David may have a lamp in Jerusalem. His conquests in Edom and Zobah are the background to the adversaries Hadad and Rezon.

l: Jeroboam the son of Nebat, The First Book of Kings, Chapter 11
s: Jeroboam, an Ephraimite and servant of Solomon, was a mighty man of valor whom Solomon put in charge of the labor of the house of Joseph. Ahijah told him he would receive ten tribes and reign over Israel, with a sure house if he walked in the LORD's ways. He lifted his hand against the king, and when Solomon sought to kill him he fled to Shishak in Egypt until Solomon died.

l: Ahijah the Shilonite, The First Book of Kings, Chapter 11
s: Ahijah the prophet met Jeroboam alone in a field, tore his new garment into twelve pieces, and gave Jeroboam ten. He delivered the LORD's message that the kingdom would be torn from Solomon's house, with one tribe remaining.

l: Hadad the Edomite, The First Book of Kings, Chapter 11
s: Hadad, of the king's offspring in Edom, fled to Egypt as a child after Joab struck every male in Edom. He found favor with Pharaoh, married the sister of Tahpenes the queen, and had a son, Genubath. After hearing that David and Joab were dead, he asked to return to his own country, and the LORD raised him up as an adversary to Solomon.

l: Rezon the son of Eliada, The First Book of Kings, Chapter 11
s: Rezon had fled from his lord Hadadezer king of Zobah, gathered men and became captain of a troop, and settled in Damascus. God raised him up as an adversary to Solomon, and he abhorred Israel and reigned over Syria.

l: Solomon's foreign wives, The First Book of Kings, Chapter 11
s: Solomon's foreign wives, from Moabite, Ammonite, Edomite, Sidonian, and Hittite peoples along with Pharaoh's daughter, turned his heart away after other gods in his old age. Solomon built high places for them, and they burned incense and sacrificed to their gods.

l: Israel, The First Book of Kings, Chapter 11
s: Israel had been told by the LORD not to mingle with the nations whose women Solomon loved. It suffered the adversary Rezon, who abhorred it, and is the people over whom Jeroboam is promised kingship through ten tribes.

l: the kingdom, The First Book of Kings, Chapter 11
s: The LORD declares he will tear the kingdom from Solomon, but not in his days; it will be torn from his son's hand, with one tribe left for David's and Jerusalem's sake. Ahijah's twelve-piece garment symbolizes the split, with ten tribes going to Jeroboam.

l: Solomon's idolatry and its punishment, The First Book of Kings, Chapter 11
s: Solomon followed Ashtoreth, Milcom, Chemosh, and Molech and built high places for his wives' gods, doing evil in the LORD's sight. The punishment is the loss of the kingdom's ten tribes from his son's hand, along with the adversaries Hadad and Rezon and the rise of Jeroboam, with mercy shown for David's sake.

l: The First Book of Kings, The First Book of Kings, Chapter 12
s: Rehoboam goes to Shechem to be made king, where Jeroboam and Israel ask him to lighten the heavy yoke Solomon imposed. Rehoboam rejects the old men's advice to serve the people and follows the young men's advice to threaten harsher treatment, which the text says the LORD brought about to fulfill his word spoken by Ahijah. Israel rebels, stones Adoram to death, and makes Jeroboam king, leaving only Judah (with Benjamin) loyal to Rehoboam. Rehoboam assembles 180,000 warriors, but Shemaiah relays the LORD's command not to fight, and they return home. Jeroboam fortifies Shechem and Penuel, then fearing the people will return to Rehoboam, makes two golden calves for Bethel and Dan, appoints non-Levite priests, and institutes his own feast in the eighth month.

l: Rehoboam, The First Book of Kings, Chapter 12
s: Rehoboam went to Shechem to be made king, took counsel from the old men and then the young men, and rejected the old men's advice. He answered Israel roughly, threatening more yoke and scorpions, lost the northern tribes, and fled to Jerusalem after Adoram was stoned. He assembled 180,000 warriors to fight Israel but obeyed the LORD's word through Shemaiah and went home.

l: Jeroboam the son of Nebat, The First Book of Kings, Chapter 12
s: Jeroboam, who had fled to Egypt from Solomon, was called back and spoke for the assembly to Rehoboam, then was made king over all Israel. He built Shechem and Penuel, and fearing the people would return to Rehoboam, made two golden calves, set them in Bethel and Dan, appointed non-Levite priests, and ordained a feast of his own devising.

l: Israel, The First Book of Kings, Chapter 12
s: Israel assembled at Shechem to make Rehoboam king but asked for a lighter yoke, and when refused, declared they had no portion in David and departed to their tents. They stoned Adoram to death, rebelled against David's house, and made Jeroboam king. They then followed Jeroboam's calf worship at Bethel and Dan.

l: old men (Solomon's counselors), The First Book of Kings, Chapter 12
s: The old men who had stood before Solomon advised Rehoboam to be a servant to the people and answer with good words, so that they would be his servants forever. Rehoboam abandoned their counsel.

l: young men (Rehoboam's companions), The First Book of Kings, Chapter 12
s: The young men who had grown up with Rehoboam advised him to say his little finger was thicker than his father's waist and that he would add to the yoke and chastise with scorpions. Rehoboam followed their counsel and spoke those words to the people.

l: yoke (Solomon's burden on Israel), The First Book of Kings, Chapter 12
s: The people called Solomon's yoke and hard service difficult and asked Rehoboam to lighten it in exchange for their service. Rehoboam instead promised to add to it, which triggered Israel's rebellion.

l: the LORD, The First Book of Kings, Chapter 12
s: The LORD brought about Rehoboam's refusal to listen in order to establish his word spoken by Ahijah the Shilonite to Jeroboam. Through Shemaiah he forbade Judah and Benjamin from fighting their brothers, saying the thing was from him, and they obeyed.

l: Judah, The First Book of Kings, Chapter 12
s: Judah, with Benjamin, remained with Rehoboam after Israel rebelled; Israelites living in Judah's cities were also ruled by him. Rehoboam assembled the house of Judah and Benjamin for war but they turned back at the LORD's word. Jerusalem in Judah was the place of the LORD's house that Jeroboam feared would draw the people back.

l: golden calves, The First Book of Kings, Chapter 12
s: Jeroboam made two golden calves, telling the people they were the gods who brought Israel out of Egypt, and set one in Bethel and the other in Dan. The text calls this a sin, as people went as far as Dan to worship.

l: Bethel, The First Book of Kings, Chapter 12
s: Bethel was where Jeroboam set one of the golden calves and built an altar. There he placed priests of the high places, sacrificed to the calves, and burned incense at a feast on the fifteenth day of the eighth month.

l: division of the kingdom, The First Book of Kings, Chapter 12
s: The kingdom divided when Israel rejected Rehoboam and David's house, making Jeroboam king, while only Judah (with Benjamin) stayed with Rehoboam. The text presents it as brought about by the LORD, who told Judah not to fight to reverse it.

l: The First Book of Kings, The First Book of Kings, Chapter 13
s: A man of God from Judah comes to Bethel by the LORD's word and prophesies against the altar where King Jeroboam is burning incense, foretelling that a son of David's house named Josiah will sacrifice the high-place priests on it. Jeroboam's outstretched hand withers when he orders the man seized, and the altar splits as the sign foretold; the man of God intercedes and the hand is restored, but he refuses the king's invitation to eat because the LORD commanded him not to eat, drink, or return by the same way. An old prophet of Bethel pursues him and, lying that an angel told him to, persuades him to eat at his house. The LORD then pronounces judgment through the old prophet, and a lion kills the man of God on the road, yet does not eat the body or harm the donkey. The old prophet buries him in his own grave, asks to be buried beside him, and affirms the prophecy, while Jeroboam persists in making high-place priests, which brings his house to ruin.

l: man of God (from Judah), The First Book of Kings, Chapter 13
s: The man of God came from Judah to Bethel by the LORD's word, prophesied against the altar, gave a sign, and interceded so that Jeroboam's hand was restored. He refused the king's offer of food, citing the LORD's command, but was deceived by the old prophet's lie, went back and ate and drank, and was told his body would not reach his fathers' tomb. A lion killed him on the road, and he was buried in the old prophet's own grave with mourning.

l: Jeroboam the son of Nebat, The First Book of Kings, Chapter 13
s: Jeroboam stood at the Bethel altar to burn incense and ordered the man of God seized, whereupon his hand dried up until the man of God interceded and it was restored. He offered the man of God a meal and a reward, which was refused. Afterward he did not turn from his evil way and kept making priests of the high places from any who wanted it, a sin that doomed his house to be cut off and destroyed.

l: old prophet (of Bethel), The First Book of Kings, Chapter 13
s: The old prophet of Bethel learned of the man of God from his sons, rode after him on a donkey, and lied that an angel had told him to bring him home to eat and drink. When the LORD's word came at the table, he announced the judgment to the man of God. After the lion's attack he retrieved the body, buried it in his own grave, mourned him as 'my brother,' and told his sons to bury him beside the man of God, affirming that the prophecy would happen.

l: the LORD, The First Book of Kings, Chapter 13
s: The LORD sent the man of God to Bethel with a word against the altar and gave him the command not to eat, drink, or return by the same way. The sign he spoke came true as the altar split and Jeroboam's hand withered and was restored. He spoke judgment through the old prophet on the disobedient man of God and delivered him to a lion, and the passage ends with Jeroboam's sin bringing destruction on his house.

l: Bethel, The First Book of Kings, Chapter 13
s: Bethel is the place where Jeroboam's altar stands and where the man of God delivers his prophecy against it. It is also where the old prophet lives and where the man of God was forbidden to eat bread or drink water. The prophecy extends against all the high-place houses in the cities of Samaria.

l: altar (at Bethel), The First Book of Kings, Chapter 13
s: The altar at Bethel is where Jeroboam stood to burn incense and is the object of the man of God's cry. It is prophesied that a son of David's house named Josiah will sacrifice the high-place priests on it and burn men's bones there. As the promised sign, it is split apart and its ashes are poured out.

l: lion, The First Book of Kings, Chapter 13
s: A lion met the man of God on the road after he left the old prophet's house and killed him. It then stood by the body beside the donkey, neither eating the body nor mauling the donkey. Its behavior was seen by passersby and was taken as the LORD's fulfillment of his word.

l: commandment against eating and drinking in Bethel, The First Book of Kings, Chapter 13
s: The LORD commanded the man of God not to eat bread, drink water, or return by the way he came. He kept it when refusing the king's offer, restating it to the old prophet, but broke it after the old prophet's lie that an angel had countermanded it. Breaking it brought the declaration that his body would not reach his fathers' tomb, and his death by the lion.

l: The First Book of Kings, The First Book of Kings, Chapter 14
s: Jeroboam's son Abijah falls sick, and Jeroboam sends his disguised wife to the blind prophet Ahijah at Shiloh with bread, cakes, and honey. The LORD warns Ahijah, who exposes her and delivers a judgment: Jeroboam's house will be utterly swept away for idolatry, a new king will cut it off, and Israel will be uprooted and scattered beyond the River. The child dies as she reaches the threshold at Tirzah, and all Israel mourns and buries him, as foretold. Jeroboam reigns twenty-two years and is succeeded by his son Nadab. The chapter then turns to Rehoboam of Judah, whose people practice idolatry and sodomy, whose treasures Shishak king of Egypt takes in his fifth year, and who dies after seventeen years, succeeded by his son Abijam.

l: Jeroboam the son of Nebat, The First Book of Kings, Chapter 14
s: Jeroboam sends his wife in disguise to the prophet Ahijah to learn what will become of his sick son Abijah. He is condemned through Ahijah for doing evil above all before him, making other gods and molten images, and casting the LORD behind his back. He reigns twenty-two years, sleeps with his fathers, and is succeeded by his son Nadab, and he is at continual war with Rehoboam.

l: Jeroboam's wife, The First Book of Kings, Chapter 14
s: Jeroboam's wife disguises herself and travels to Shiloh with ten loaves, cakes, and a jar of honey. Ahijah recognizes her by the sound of her feet and gives her heavy news. She returns to Tirzah, and the child dies as she reaches the threshold of the house.

l: Abijah, The First Book of Kings, Chapter 14
s: Abijah, son of Jeroboam, becomes sick, prompting his father to seek word from Ahijah. He is the only one of Jeroboam's house to receive burial and mourning, because some good toward the LORD was found in him. He dies as his mother enters the city, and all Israel buries and mourns him.

l: Ahijah the Shilonite, The First Book of Kings, Chapter 14
s: Ahijah is the prophet at Shiloh who earlier said Jeroboam would be king, and he is now unable to see because of his age. Warned by the LORD, he identifies Jeroboam's disguised wife and delivers the LORD's judgment on Jeroboam's house and on Israel. His word about the child is fulfilled.

l: the LORD, The First Book of Kings, Chapter 14
s: The LORD tells Ahijah that Jeroboam's wife is coming in disguise and what to say. He pronounces judgment on Jeroboam for exalting him yet being rewarded with idolatry, and promises to raise up a king to cut off Jeroboam's house and to strike and scatter Israel. He is also named as having chosen Jerusalem to put his name there, and is provoked to jealousy by Judah's sins.

l: Israel, The First Book of Kings, Chapter 14
s: Israel is told it will be struck like a reed shaken in the water, rooted up from the good land given to its fathers, and scattered beyond the River because of its Asherah poles and the sins of Jeroboam. All Israel mourns and buries Abijah. A new king is foretold to rise over it.

l: house of Jeroboam, The First Book of Kings, Chapter 14
s: The house of Jeroboam is condemned to be cut off and swept away like dung, with those who die in the city eaten by dogs and those in the field by birds. Only Abijah will come to the grave. A king raised up by the LORD will cut the house off, and Nadab succeeds Jeroboam as king.

l: Rehoboam, The First Book of Kings, Chapter 14
s: Rehoboam, son of Solomon and of Naamah the Ammonitess, begins to reign in Judah at forty-one and reigns seventeen years in Jerusalem. When Shishak takes the treasures, he replaces the gold shields with bronze ones guarded by the captains of the guard. He is at war with Jeroboam continually, and when he dies he is buried in David's city and succeeded by his son Abijam.

l: Judah, The First Book of Kings, Chapter 14
s: Judah does evil in the LORD's sight, provoking him to jealousy beyond what their fathers did. They build high places, sacred pillars, and Asherah poles on every high hill and under every green tree, and sodomites are in the land, following the abominations of the nations the LORD drove out. In Rehoboam's fifth year Shishak king of Egypt comes up against Jerusalem and takes its treasures.

l: Abijah's death and burial, The First Book of Kings, Chapter 14
s: Abijah dies just as his mother reaches the threshold of the house at Tirzah, fulfilling Ahijah's word. All Israel buries and mourns him according to the LORD's word. He alone of Jeroboam's house is given a grave because some good toward the LORD was found in him.

l: Ahijah's prophecy against Jeroboam's house, The First Book of Kings, Chapter 14
s: Ahijah, speaking the LORD's words, charges Jeroboam with idolatry despite being exalted and given the torn kingdom, and announces that his house will be cut off and swept away like dung. He foretells the child's death on her return, a king raised up to end the house, and Israel's being uprooted and scattered beyond the River. The child's death and burial and Jeroboam's death are recorded as it begins to be fulfilled.

l: The First Book of Kings, The First Book of Kings, Chapter 15
s: Chapter 15 covers the reigns of Abijam and Asa over Judah and of Nadab and Baasha over Israel. Abijam reigned three years, walking in his father's sins, though the LORD preserved his line for David's sake. Asa reigned forty-one years and did right: he removed the sodomites, idols, and his mother Maacah's Asherah image, but he left the high places. When Baasha of Israel built Ramah against Judah, Asa sent the temple and royal treasures to Ben Hadad of Syria, who attacked northern Israelite cities, so Baasha stopped and Asa used the Ramah materials to build Geba and Mizpah. In Israel, Baasha killed Nadab son of Jeroboam at Gibbethon, wiped out Jeroboam's house as the LORD had spoken through Ahijah, and reigned twenty-four years in Tirzah doing evil.

l: Abijam, The First Book of Kings, Chapter 15
s: Abijam began to reign over Judah in Jeroboam's eighteenth year and reigned three years in Jerusalem; his mother was Maacah the daughter of Abishalom. He walked in his father's sins and his heart was not perfect with the LORD, yet for David's sake the LORD gave him a lamp in Jerusalem, a son to follow him. He was at war with Jeroboam, slept with his fathers, was buried in David's city, and was succeeded by his son Asa.

l: Jeroboam the son of Nebat, The First Book of Kings, Chapter 15
s: Jeroboam was king of Israel when Abijam began to reign in his eighteenth year and when Asa began in his twentieth year. War continued between him and Abijam. His sins, by which he made Israel sin, were the standard for his son Nadab and for Baasha, and his whole house was destroyed by Baasha according to the LORD's word through Ahijah.

l: Asa, The First Book of Kings, Chapter 15
s: Asa reigned forty-one years over Judah and did right in the LORD's eyes like David: he put away the sodomites and idols, removed his mother Maacah from being queen for making an image for an Asherah, and burned the image at the Kidron. He left the high places, though his heart was perfect with the LORD all his days. Facing Baasha's building of Ramah, he bribed Ben Hadad with temple and palace treasure, then used Ramah's stones and timber to build Geba and Mizpah; in old age he was diseased in his feet, and Jehoshaphat his son succeeded him.

l: Baasha, The First Book of Kings, Chapter 15
s: Baasha son of Ahijah, of the house of Issachar, conspired against Nadab, struck him at Gibbethon in Asa's third year, and became king over all Israel, reigning twenty-four years in Tirzah. He destroyed all of Jeroboam's house, leaving no one who breathed. He did evil, walking in Jeroboam's way. He fought Asa all their days, built Ramah against Judah, and stopped and went to live in Tirzah when Ben Hadad attacked.

l: Nadab, The First Book of Kings, Chapter 15
s: Nadab son of Jeroboam began to reign over Israel in Asa's second year and reigned two years. He did evil in the LORD's sight, walking in his father's way and sin. While he and all Israel besieged Gibbethon, Baasha conspired against and killed him and took his throne.

l: Ben Hadad, The First Book of Kings, Chapter 15
s: Ben Hadad, son of Tabrimmon, son of Hezion, was king of Syria and lived at Damascus. Asa sent him silver and gold and asked him to break his treaty with Baasha. He listened, sending his army captains against Israel, where they struck Ijon, Dan, Abel Beth Maacah, all Chinneroth, and the land of Naphtali.

l: the LORD, The First Book of Kings, Chapter 15
s: The LORD gave Abijam a lamp in Jerusalem for David's sake, so that his son would succeed him and Jerusalem would be established. Asa did right in his eyes, and the destruction of Jeroboam's house fulfilled what the LORD had spoken by Ahijah the Shilonite. Jeroboam's sins had provoked the LORD, the God of Israel, to anger.

l: Judah, The First Book of Kings, Chapter 15
s: Judah was ruled first by Abijam for three years and then by Asa for forty-one years, with Jehoshaphat succeeding Asa. It was at war with Israel and was pressed by Baasha's building of Ramah. Asa called all of Judah, exempting no one, to carry away Ramah's stones and timber.

l: Israel, The First Book of Kings, Chapter 15
s: Israel was ruled by Jeroboam, then Nadab, then Baasha, who reigned from Tirzah. It was at war with Judah, and its northern cities and the land of Naphtali were struck by Ben Hadad. Both Nadab and Baasha did evil, following Jeroboam's sin with which he made Israel sin.

l: Ramah, The First Book of Kings, Chapter 15
s: Baasha built Ramah to keep anyone from going out or coming in to Asa king of Judah. When Ben Hadad attacked Israel, Baasha stopped building it. Asa had all Judah carry away its stones and timber and used them to build Geba of Benjamin and Mizpah.

l: war between Asa and Baasha, The First Book of Kings, Chapter 15
s: The text states twice that there was war between Asa and Baasha all their days. It included Baasha's building of Ramah to blockade Judah, Asa's payment to Ben Hadad of Syria to break his treaty with Baasha, and Ben Hadad's attack on Israelite cities. The result was that Baasha abandoned Ramah and Asa took its materials.

l: The First Book of Kings, The First Book of Kings, Chapter 16
s: The LORD's word comes through Jehu the son of Hanani against Baasha of Israel for walking in Jeroboam's way, and after Baasha dies his son Elah reigns in Tirzah. Elah is killed while drunk by his chariot captain Zimri, who wipes out Baasha's house, then reigns only seven days before the army makes Omri king, and Zimri burns the king's house over himself when Tirzah is besieged. Israel is briefly split between followers of Tibni and Omri until Omri prevails; he buys the hill of Samaria from Shemer and builds the city. Omri's son Ahab becomes king, marries Jezebel daughter of Ethbaal, serves Baal, builds an altar and Asherah, and does more evil than any earlier king. The chapter closes with Hiel the Bethelite rebuilding Jericho at the cost of his sons, according to the LORD's word by Joshua.

l: the LORD, The First Book of Kings, Chapter 16
s: The LORD sends his word through Jehu against Baasha, declaring he will sweep away Baasha and his house because Baasha walked in Jeroboam's way and made Israel sin. His word is fulfilled when Zimri destroys Baasha's house, and again when Hiel loses his sons while rebuilding Jericho, as spoken by Joshua. He is provoked to anger by the sins of Baasha, Elah, Zimri, Omri and especially Ahab.

l: Jehu the son of Hanani, The First Book of Kings, Chapter 16
s: Jehu the son of Hanani, called a prophet, receives and delivers the LORD's word against Baasha and his house. The prophecy foretells that Baasha's house will be swept away like the house of Jeroboam, and it is later fulfilled.

l: Baasha, The First Book of Kings, Chapter 16
s: Baasha is condemned by the LORD through Jehu for walking in Jeroboam's way, making Israel sin, and striking down the house of Jeroboam. He sleeps with his fathers, is buried in Tirzah, and is succeeded by his son Elah.

l: house of Baasha, The First Book of Kings, Chapter 16
s: The house of Baasha is prophesied to be swept away, with its dead eaten by dogs in the city and birds in the field. Zimri fulfills this by killing all of Baasha's house, leaving no male relative or friend, because of the sins of Baasha and Elah.

l: Israel, The First Book of Kings, Chapter 16
s: Israel is led into sin by Baasha, Elah, Zimri, Omri and Ahab, who follow Jeroboam's way. It sees three changes of king in quick succession, the army proclaims Omri king in the camp at Gibbethon, and the people are then divided between Tibni and Omri until Omri prevails.

l: Elah, The First Book of Kings, Chapter 16
s: Elah son of Baasha begins to reign over Israel in Tirzah in Asa's twenty-sixth year and reigns two years. While drinking himself drunk in Arza's house, he is struck down and killed by his servant Zimri.

l: Zimri, The First Book of Kings, Chapter 16
s: Zimri, captain of half of Elah's chariots, conspires against Elah, kills him in Tirzah, and reigns in his place. He destroys all of Baasha's house, but reigns only seven days; when Tirzah is besieged by Omri, he burns the king's house over himself and dies for his sins.

l: Omri, The First Book of Kings, Chapter 16
s: Omri, captain of the army, is made king by all Israel in the camp at Gibbethon, then besieges Tirzah and ends Zimri's reign. After overcoming Tibni's faction he reigns twelve years, buys the hill Samaria from Shemer for two talents of silver and builds the city. He does evil above all before him, walks in Jeroboam's way, dies and is buried in Samaria, and Ahab succeeds him.

l: Ahab, The First Book of Kings, Chapter 16
s: Ahab begins to reign in Asa's thirty-eighth year and reigns twenty-two years in Samaria. He does evil above all before him, marries Jezebel daughter of Ethbaal, serves and worships Baal, raises an altar for Baal in Samaria, and makes the Asherah, provoking the LORD more than any earlier king of Israel.

l: Tirzah, The First Book of Kings, Chapter 16
s: Tirzah is the royal city where Baasha is buried and where Elah reigns and is killed in Arza's house. Zimri reigns there seven days, Omri besieges it, and Zimri burns the king's house there. Omri reigns six years in Tirzah before moving to Samaria.

l: Samaria, The First Book of Kings, Chapter 16
s: Samaria is a hill that Omri buys from Shemer for two talents of silver, builds on, and names after Shemer. Omri is buried there, and Ahab reigns from there and raises an altar for Baal in the house of Baal he built in Samaria.

l: conspiracy of Zimri against Elah, The First Book of Kings, Chapter 16
s: Zimri, captain of half of Elah's chariots, conspires against his master and kills him in Tirzah while Elah is drunk in Arza's house. It fulfills the LORD's word against Baasha's house, but when the army at Gibbethon hears of it they make Omri king, and Zimri's reign ends in seven days.

l: The First Book of Kings, The First Book of Kings, Chapter 17
s: Elijah the Tishbite, a settler of Gilead, tells Ahab that there will be no dew or rain except by his word. The LORD sends him to hide by the brook Cherith, where ravens feed him, until the brook dries up. The LORD then sends him to Zarephath, where a widow gathering sticks feeds him from her last meal and oil, which then do not run out. When the widow's son becomes sick and stops breathing, Elijah carries him to his room, stretches himself on him three times, and prays, and the child revives. The widow then declares that Elijah is a man of God and that the LORD's word in his mouth is truth.

l: Elijah the Tishbite, The First Book of Kings, Chapter 17
s: Elijah, a settler of Gilead, tells Ahab there will be no dew or rain except by his word, then obeys the LORD's commands to live by the brook Cherith and later in Zarephath. He promises the widow that her meal and oil will not run out, and he prays over her dead son, stretching himself on the child three times, until the child revives. The widow concludes that he is a man of God.

l: the LORD, The First Book of Kings, Chapter 17
s: The LORD speaks to Elijah, directing him to Cherith, where he commands ravens to feed him, and then to Zarephath, where he has commanded a widow to sustain him. He keeps the widow's jars from running out as Elijah promised and listens to Elijah's voice, returning the child's soul so that he revives.

l: Zarephath, The First Book of Kings, Chapter 17
s: Zarephath is a city belonging to Sidon, to which the LORD sends Elijah after the brook dries up. Its gate is where Elijah meets the widow gathering sticks, and it is where he stays in her house.

l: widow (of Zarephath), The First Book of Kings, Chapter 17
s: The widow is found gathering sticks at the city gate and says she has only a handful of meal and a little oil, intending to bake a last meal for herself and her son before they die. She obeys Elijah, makes him a cake first, and her household eats for many days. When her son dies she accuses Elijah of bringing her sin to memory, but after he is revived she says she knows he is a man of God and that the LORD's word in his mouth is truth.

l: son (the widow's son), The First Book of Kings, Chapter 17
s: The widow's son becomes so sick that no breath is left in him. Elijah takes him from his mother's bosom, lays him on his own bed upstairs, and prays over him, and the child's soul comes back into him and he revives. Elijah then hands him back to his mother, saying he lives.

l: drought (no dew nor rain), The First Book of Kings, Chapter 17
s: Elijah announces to Ahab that there will be no dew or rain for these years except according to his word. The effects appear when the brook Cherith dries up because there is no rain in the land. The LORD's promise to the widow that her jars will not fail lasts until the day he sends rain on the earth.

l: jar of meal, The First Book of Kings, Chapter 17
s: The widow has only a handful of meal in a jar, which she plans to bake for herself and her son. After Elijah promises in the LORD's name that it will not run out, it does not run out, according to the LORD's word spoken by Elijah.

l: jar of oil, The First Book of Kings, Chapter 17
s: The widow has a little oil in a jar, which she plans to use with the last of her meal. Elijah promises that it will not fail until the LORD sends rain, and it does not fail, according to the LORD's word spoken by Elijah.

l: resurrection of the widow's son, The First Book of Kings, Chapter 17
s: After the widow's son stops breathing, Elijah carries him to the upper room, cries to the LORD, and stretches himself on the child three times, asking that his soul come into him again. The LORD listens, the child's soul returns and he revives, and Elijah gives him back to his mother, which leads her to affirm that Elijah is a man of God.

l: The First Book of Kings, The First Book of Kings, Chapter 18
s: In the third year of famine, the LORD tells Elijah to show himself to Ahab so that rain may come. Elijah meets Ahab's household head Obadiah, who fears the LORD and had hidden one hundred prophets from Jezebel, and persuades him to tell Ahab that Elijah is there. Elijah rebukes Ahab for following the Baals and has all Israel and the prophets of Baal and the Asherah gathered at Mount Carmel, where he proposes a contest in which the God who answers by fire is God. The prophets of Baal call on him from morning until evening with no answer, while Elijah rebuilds the LORD's altar, soaks the offering with water, and prays, and the LORD's fire consumes everything. The people declare the LORD is God, Elijah has the prophets of Baal killed at the brook Kishon, and a great rain comes, after which Elijah runs ahead of Ahab's chariot to Jezreel.

l: Elijah the Tishbite, The First Book of Kings, Chapter 18
s: Elijah is told by the LORD to show himself to Ahab, persuades the fearful Obadiah to announce him, and tells Ahab that Ahab and his father's house have troubled Israel by following the Baals. On Mount Carmel he challenges the people to choose between the LORD and Baal, mocks the prophets of Baal, rebuilds the altar, prays, and sees the LORD's fire fall, then has the prophets of Baal killed. He prays for rain with his face between his knees, sends his servant to look at the sea seven times, and, with the LORD's hand on him, runs ahead of Ahab to the entrance of Jezreel.

l: Ahab, The First Book of Kings, Chapter 18
s: Ahab sends Obadiah to search the springs and brooks for grass for the animals, and had sent to every nation and kingdom seeking Elijah. He calls Elijah a troubler of Israel, is rebuked as the one who forsook the LORD's commandments, and gathers Israel and the prophets to Mount Carmel. After the contest Elijah tells him to eat and drink, and he rides to Jezreel in the rain.

l: Obadiah, The First Book of Kings, Chapter 18
s: Obadiah is over Ahab's household and fears the LORD greatly; he had hidden one hundred prophets, fifty to a cave, and fed them when Jezebel cut off the LORD's prophets. He fears Ahab will kill him if Elijah vanishes after being announced, but after Elijah swears to show himself that day, he goes and tells Ahab.

l: the LORD, The First Book of Kings, Chapter 18
s: The LORD sends his word to Elijah promising rain and answers Elijah's prayer on Carmel by sending fire that consumes the offering, wood, stones, dust, and water. The people respond by declaring that the LORD is God. His hand is on Elijah as he runs to Jezreel.

l: Baal, The First Book of Kings, Chapter 18
s: Baal is the god the people are urged to follow if he is God, and Ahab and his father's house are said to have followed the Baals. When his prophets call on him from morning until evening, there is no voice, no answer, and nobody paying attention. Elijah mocks that he may be deep in thought, away, on a journey, or asleep.

l: prophets of Baal (Baal), The First Book of Kings, Chapter 18
s: Four hundred fifty prophets of Baal, along with four hundred prophets of the Asherah who eat at Jezebel's table, are gathered to Mount Carmel. They prepare a bull, call on Baal from morning until the evening offering, leap about the altar, and cut themselves with knives and lances, but receive no answer. After the LORD's fire falls, Elijah has them seized and killed at the brook Kishon.

l: Israel, The First Book of Kings, Chapter 18
s: Israel is accused by Ahab of being troubled by Elijah, while Elijah says Ahab has troubled it. All the people are gathered to Mount Carmel, stay silent when asked how long they will waver, and agree to the fire test. After seeing the fire they fall on their faces and declare that the LORD is God. Elijah's twelve stones represent the tribes of the sons of Jacob, to whom the name Israel was given.

l: Mount Carmel, The First Book of Kings, Chapter 18
s: Mount Carmel is where Ahab gathers all Israel and the prophets of Baal and of the Asherah at Elijah's demand. It is the site of the contest and the fire from the LORD. Afterward Elijah goes up to its top to bow down and pray for rain.

l: contest on Mount Carmel, The First Book of Kings, Chapter 18
s: Elijah proposes that each side prepare a bull on wood with no fire and that the God who answers by fire be God, and the people agree. The prophets of Baal call from morning to the evening offering without answer. Elijah then offers his bull on a soaked altar, the LORD's fire falls, and the people acknowledge the LORD as God.

l: altar of the LORD, The First Book of Kings, Chapter 18
s: The LORD's altar had been thrown down, and Elijah repairs it. He builds it with twelve stones, digs a trench around it, arranges the wood and the cut bull, and has water poured over it three times until the trench is filled. The LORD's fire then consumes the offering, wood, stones, and dust.

l: fire from the LORD, The First Book of Kings, Chapter 18
s: After Elijah's prayer at the evening offering, the LORD's fire falls and consumes the burnt offering, the wood, the stones, and the dust, and licks up the water in the trench. It leads the people to fall on their faces and declare that the LORD is God.

l: rain, The First Book of Kings, Chapter 18
s: The LORD promises to send rain on the earth in the third year of famine. After the contest Elijah tells Ahab he hears the sound of abundance of rain, and his servant on the seventh look sees a small cloud like a man's hand rising from the sea. Soon the sky grows black with clouds and wind and a great rain falls.

l: The First Book of Kings, The First Book of Kings, Chapter 19
s: Ahab reports to Jezebel what Elijah has done, and she sends a messenger vowing to kill Elijah by the next day. Elijah flees to Beersheba in Judah, leaves his servant, and goes a day into the wilderness, where he sits under a juniper tree and asks to die. An angel twice feeds him, and he travels forty days and nights in that strength to Horeb, God's Mountain. There the LORD questions him in a cave and shows him a wind, an earthquake, and a fire, none containing the LORD, followed by a still small voice; Elijah twice gives the same complaint. The LORD sends him to anoint Hazael, Jehu, and Elisha, says seven thousand in Israel have not bowed to Baal, and Elijah then finds Elisha plowing, throws his mantle on him, and Elisha makes a farewell feast with his oxen and follows him.

l: Elijah the Tishbite, The First Book of Kings, Chapter 19
s: Elijah flees Jezebel's threat to Beersheba and then into the wilderness, where he asks the LORD to take his life. Strengthened by food from an angel, he goes to Horeb, twice tells the LORD that he alone is left and is sought for death, and is commanded to anoint Hazael, Jehu, and Elisha. He puts his mantle on Elisha, who then follows and serves him.

l: Jezebel, The First Book of Kings, Chapter 19
s: Jezebel hears from Ahab all that Elijah did, including the killing of the prophets with the sword. She sends a messenger to Elijah swearing by the gods that she will make his life like one of theirs by about the same time the next day.

l: the LORD, The First Book of Kings, Chapter 19
s: The LORD's word comes to Elijah at Horeb, asking twice what he is doing there. He passes by but is not in the wind, earthquake, or fire, and then speaks after the still small voice. He commands Elijah to anoint Hazael, Jehu, and Elisha, says Jehu and Elisha will kill those who escape Hazael's sword, and declares he has reserved seven thousand in Israel who have not bowed to Baal.

l: Elisha, The First Book of Kings, Chapter 19
s: Elisha, son of Shaphat of Abel Meholah, is found plowing with twelve yoke of oxen, himself with the twelfth, when Elijah puts his mantle on him. He asks to kiss his father and mother first, then kills the yoke of oxen, boils the meat with the oxen's equipment, and gives it to the people to eat. He then goes after Elijah and serves him.

l: Horeb, The First Book of Kings, Chapter 19
s: Horeb, called God's Mountain, is where Elijah arrives after forty days and nights of travel. He camps in a cave there, and the LORD's word comes to him and the LORD passes by on the mountain.

l: angel (the LORD's angel), The First Book of Kings, Chapter 19
s: The LORD's angel touches Elijah as he sleeps under the juniper tree and tells him to arise and eat, and a cake baked on the coals and a jar of water are at his head. The angel comes a second time, saying the journey is too great for him, and Elijah goes in the strength of that food.

l: wind, earthquake, and fire (theophany at Horeb), The First Book of Kings, Chapter 19
s: As the LORD passes by, a great and strong wind tears the mountains and breaks rocks in pieces, then an earthquake comes, then a fire passes. The text states that the LORD was not in the wind, the earthquake, or the fire.

l: still small voice, The First Book of Kings, Chapter 19
s: After the fire, there is a still small voice. When Elijah hears it, he wraps his face in his mantle, goes out, and stands in the entrance of the cave, where a voice asks him what he is doing there.

l: mantle (Elijah's mantle), The First Book of Kings, Chapter 19
s: Elijah wraps his face in his mantle when he hears the still small voice. Later he puts his mantle on Elisha as he passes him plowing, after which Elisha leaves the oxen and runs after him.

l: The First Book of Kings, The First Book of Kings, Chapter 20
s: Ben Hadad, king of Syria, besieges Samaria with thirty-two allied kings and demands Ahab's silver, gold, wives, and children; Ahab yields at first but refuses the second demand on the elders' advice. A prophet promises victory, and the young men of the princes of the provinces lead Israel out and rout the Syrians while Ben Hadad is drinking. The next year Ben Hadad attacks at Aphek, believing the LORD is only a god of the hills, and Israel kills one hundred thousand Syrians in one day. Ahab spares Ben Hadad and makes a covenant with him, and a prophet who disguises himself announces that Ahab's life and people will take the place of Ben Hadad's because he let go the man devoted to destruction. Ahab goes home sullen and angry.

l: Ben Hadad, The First Book of Kings, Chapter 20
s: Ben Hadad, king of Syria, besieges Samaria with thirty-two kings, demands Ahab's wealth, wives, and children, and is routed while drinking himself drunk. He returns a year later to fight at Aphek on the advice of his servants, flees into an inner room after defeat, and is spared by Ahab, promising to restore cities and give Ahab streets in Damascus.

l: Ahab, The First Book of Kings, Chapter 20
s: Ahab, king of Israel, first submits to Ben Hadad's demands, then refuses the second on the elders' advice, and wins two victories after prophetic words. He calls Ben Hadad his brother, makes a covenant with him and lets him go, and is then told by a prophet that his life will take the place of Ben Hadad's life; he goes home sullen and angry.

l: Samaria, The First Book of Kings, Chapter 20
s: Samaria is the city Ben Hadad besieges and where Ahab consults the elders. Ben Hadad's father had made streets in Samaria, and Ahab returns there sullen and angry at the end.

l: Syrians, The First Book of Kings, Chapter 20
s: The Syrians flee before Israel's attack at Samaria, then reason that Israel's god is a god of the hills and regroup to fight in the plain. At Aphek one hundred thousand footmen are killed in a day, and a wall falls on twenty-seven thousand of the rest.

l: Israel, The First Book of Kings, Chapter 20
s: Israel, led by Ahab, is mustered at seven thousand and defeats the Syrians at Samaria, striking horses and chariots. At Aphek it camps like two little flocks of young goats against a Syrian army that fills the country, yet wins a great victory.

l: the LORD, The First Book of Kings, Chapter 20
s: The LORD promises through a prophet to deliver the great Syrian multitude into Ahab's hand so that Ahab will know he is the LORD. He answers the claim that he is only a god of the hills by giving victory in the valley, and he declares that Ahab's life will replace the life of the man devoted to destruction.

l: Aphek, The First Book of Kings, Chapter 20
s: Aphek is where Ben Hadad musters the Syrians to fight Israel at the return of the year. After the defeat the survivors flee into its city, where a wall falls on twenty-seven thousand men and Ben Hadad hides in an inner room.

l: prophet (who spoke to Ahab), The First Book of Kings, Chapter 20
s: A prophet tells Ahab the LORD will deliver the great multitude, names the young men of the princes of the provinces as the means, and says Ahab should begin the battle. He later warns Ahab to strengthen himself because the king of Syria will return at the year's end. A man of God then gives the word before Aphek.

l: young men of the princes of the provinces, The First Book of Kings, Chapter 20
s: These young men, two hundred and thirty-two in number, are named by the LORD as the means of victory and go out first at noon. Each kills his man, and the Syrians flee.

l: prophet (son of the prophets who disguised himself), The First Book of Kings, Chapter 20
s: This prophet asks a fellow to strike him; the first refuses and is killed by a lion, and the second strikes and wounds him. He disguises himself with a headband over his eyes, tells Ahab a story about a lost prisoner so that Ahab pronounces his own judgment, then reveals himself and announces the LORD's sentence on Ahab.

l: siege of Samaria, The First Book of Kings, Chapter 20
s: Ben Hadad and thirty-two kings besiege Samaria and send demands that Ahab give up silver, gold, wives, and children, plus a search of the houses. After Ahab refuses the second demand, the Syrians prepare to attack, but Israel sallies out at noon and routs them, and Ben Hadad escapes on a horse.

l: battle at Aphek, The First Book of Kings, Chapter 20
s: After seven days of encampment the battle is joined on the seventh day, and Israel kills one hundred thousand Syrian footmen in one day. The survivors flee into Aphek, where a wall falls on twenty-seven thousand, and Ben Hadad is left begging for his life.

l: covenant between Ahab and Ben Hadad, The First Book of Kings, Chapter 20
s: After Ben Hadad's servants plead for his life, Ahab calls him his brother, takes him into his chariot, and makes a covenant with him. Ben Hadad promises to restore cities his father took and to give Ahab streets in Damascus, and Ahab lets him go; a prophet later condemns this release.

l: The First Book of Kings, The First Book of Kings, Chapter 21
s: Ahab king of Samaria asks Naboth the Jezreelite to sell or exchange his vineyard next to the palace in Jezreel, but Naboth refuses because it is the inheritance of his fathers. Ahab sulks, and his wife Jezebel writes letters in his name to the elders and nobles of Naboth's city, instructing them to stage a fast and have two wicked fellows falsely accuse Naboth of cursing God and the king. The elders and nobles comply, Naboth is stoned to death, and Ahab goes to take possession of the vineyard. The LORD sends Elijah the Tishbite to confront Ahab, announcing that dogs will lick his blood, that his house will be swept away like those of Jeroboam and Baasha, and that dogs will eat Jezebel. When Ahab tears his clothes and humbles himself, the LORD says he will delay the evil until the days of Ahab's son.

l: Naboth the Jezreelite, The First Book of Kings, Chapter 21
s: Naboth owns a vineyard in Jezreel beside Ahab's palace and refuses to give it up, saying it is the inheritance of his fathers. He is falsely accused of cursing God and the king, carried out of the city, and stoned to death.

l: Ahab, The First Book of Kings, Chapter 21
s: Ahab asks Naboth for his vineyard, sulks and refuses to eat when refused, and lets Jezebel arrange Naboth's death before going down to take possession. Elijah confronts him with the LORD's judgment, and when Ahab tears his clothes and fasts in sackcloth, the LORD delays the evil to his son's day.

l: Jezebel, The First Book of Kings, Chapter 21
s: Jezebel rebukes Ahab's sulking and writes letters in his name, sealed with his seal, ordering a false trial and stoning of Naboth. She then tells Ahab to take the vineyard, and the LORD declares that dogs will eat her by the rampart of Jezreel.

l: Elijah the Tishbite, The First Book of Kings, Chapter 21
s: Elijah receives the LORD's word and goes to meet Ahab in Naboth's vineyard. He delivers the charge, "Have you killed and also taken possession?", and announces the coming judgment on Ahab, his house, and Jezebel.

l: the LORD, The First Book of Kings, Chapter 21
s: The LORD sends Elijah to condemn Ahab for killing Naboth and taking his vineyard, and pronounces that dogs will lick Ahab's blood and eat Jezebel. Seeing Ahab humble himself, the LORD decides to bring the evil on Ahab's house in his son's day rather than in Ahab's own days.

l: vineyard (Naboth's vineyard), The First Book of Kings, Chapter 21
s: The vineyard in Jezreel next to Ahab's palace is wanted by Ahab as a garden of herbs. Naboth refuses to give it, but after Naboth's death Ahab goes down to take possession of it, and it becomes the place of Elijah's confrontation.

l: elders and nobles (of Naboth's city), The First Book of Kings, Chapter 21
s: The elders and nobles who lived with Naboth receive Jezebel's letters and do exactly as instructed, proclaiming a fast and setting Naboth on high among the people. They carry out the false trial and stoning and then send word to Jezebel that Naboth is dead.

l: wicked fellows (false witnesses against Naboth), The First Book of Kings, Chapter 21
s: Two wicked fellows are set before Naboth at Jezebel's direction. In the presence of the people they testify falsely that Naboth cursed God and the king, which leads to his stoning.

l: Naboth's stoning, The First Book of Kings, Chapter 21
s: Naboth is stoned to death outside the city after the false testimony arranged by Jezebel's letters. Word is sent to Jezebel, who tells Ahab to seize the vineyard, and the event becomes the ground of the LORD's judgment through Elijah.

l: Judgment against Ahab's house, The First Book of Kings, Chapter 21
s: The LORD declares through Elijah that he will bring evil on Ahab, sweep away his male descendants, and make his house like those of Jeroboam and Baasha. Dogs will eat Jezebel, and those of Ahab's line who die in the city or the field will be eaten by dogs and birds, though after Ahab humbles himself the evil is postponed to his son's day.

l: The First Book of Kings, The First Book of Kings, Chapter 22
s: After three years of peace between Syria and Israel, Ahab king of Israel persuades Jehoshaphat king of Judah to join him in attacking Ramoth Gilead. Ahab's four hundred prophets, led by Zedekiah the son of Chenaanah, promise victory, but Micaiah the son of Imlah reveals that the LORD has put a lying spirit in their mouths and that Ahab will fall; Ahab imprisons him. Ahab disguises himself in battle, yet a random arrow wounds him and he dies at evening, and his blood is licked up by dogs as the LORD had said. The chapter then summarizes Jehoshaphat's reign over Judah, including his righteousness, his failed ships, and his death, and closes with Ahaziah son of Ahab ruling Israel in evil, serving Baal.

l: Ahab, The First Book of Kings, Chapter 22
s: Ahab, king of Israel, proposes taking Ramoth Gilead from Syria, hates Micaiah for prophesying evil about him, and imprisons him. He disguises himself in battle but is struck by a random arrow and dies at evening, and is buried in Samaria. His reign is closed out with a reference to the ivory house and cities he built, and Ahaziah his son succeeds him.

l: Jehoshaphat, The First Book of Kings, Chapter 22
s: Jehoshaphat, king of Judah, joins Ahab against Ramoth Gilead but asks first to inquire of the LORD and insists on hearing a prophet of the LORD. In battle he is mistaken for Ahab and cries out, and the Syrian captains turn back. His reign of twenty-five years is summarized: he walked in Asa's way, left the high places, made peace with Israel, removed the remaining sodomites, lost his ships at Ezion Geber, refused Ahaziah's offer to sail together, and died, succeeded by Jehoram.

l: Micaiah the son of Imlah, The First Book of Kings, Chapter 22
s: Micaiah is the one prophet of the LORD whom Jehoshaphat asks for; Ahab hates him because he prophesies evil. He first echoes the other prophets, then, pressed to tell the truth, foretells Israel scattered like shepherdless sheep and describes the heavenly council and the lying spirit. He is struck by Zedekiah, jailed on bread and water, and declares that if Ahab returns in peace the LORD has not spoken by him.

l: Zedekiah the son of Chenaanah, The First Book of Kings, Chapter 22
s: Zedekiah makes iron horns and prophesies that the king will push the Syrians until they are consumed. He strikes Micaiah on the cheek and mocks him, and Micaiah answers that Zedekiah will see on that day when he goes into an inner room to hide.

l: Ramoth Gilead, The First Book of Kings, Chapter 22
s: Ahab claims Ramoth Gilead as Israel's and complains that it remains in the hand of the king of Syria. Ahab and Jehoshaphat go up to it to fight, and the battle there ends with Ahab's death.

l: Israel, The First Book of Kings, Chapter 22
s: Israel is ruled by Ahab, who goes to war with Syria for Ramoth Gilead after three years of peace. Micaiah sees all Israel scattered on the mountains like sheep without a shepherd. After Ahab's death the army disperses to their cities, and Ahaziah begins to reign in Samaria.

l: Syrians, The First Book of Kings, Chapter 22
s: Syria holds Ramoth Gilead and has been at peace with Israel for three years. Its king orders his thirty-two chariot captains to fight only the king of Israel. The captains chase Jehoshaphat by mistake, then turn back, and a Syrian archer's random shot strikes Ahab.

l: the LORD, The First Book of Kings, Chapter 22
s: The LORD is said by Micaiah to sit on his throne among the army of heaven and to ask who will entice Ahab to fall at Ramoth Gilead. He accepts a spirit's plan to be a lying spirit in the mouth of Ahab's prophets and has spoken evil concerning Ahab. His word about the dogs licking Ahab's blood is fulfilled.

l: prophets of Ahab, The First Book of Kings, Chapter 22
s: About four hundred prophets gathered by Ahab all say, with one mouth, to go up to Ramoth Gilead and prosper because the LORD will deliver it to the king. Micaiah says the LORD has put a lying spirit in their mouths.

l: lying spirit (sent by the LORD to entice Ahab), The First Book of Kings, Chapter 22
s: In Micaiah's vision a spirit comes before the LORD and offers to entice Ahab by being a lying spirit in the mouth of all his prophets. The LORD says it will entice him and prevail, and tells it to go out and do so.

l: battle at Ramoth Gilead, The First Book of Kings, Chapter 22
s: Ahab and Jehoshaphat fight at Ramoth Gilead, with Ahab in disguise and Jehoshaphat in his robes. The Syrian chariot captains pursue Jehoshaphat until they see he is not the king of Israel, then a random arrow wounds Ahab. The battle increases that day, and at sunset a cry goes out for every man to return to his city and country.

l: Ahab's death, The First Book of Kings, Chapter 22
s: Ahab is struck by an arrow between the joints of his armor and is propped up in his chariot facing the Syrians until he dies at evening, his blood running into the chariot. He is buried in Samaria, and the chariot is washed at the pool of Samaria where dogs lick his blood, as the LORD had said.

l: Ahaziah the son of Ahab, The First Book of Kings, Chapter 22
s: Ahaziah asks Jehoshaphat to let his servants sail with Jehoshaphat's, but Jehoshaphat refuses. He begins to reign over Israel in Samaria in Jehoshaphat's seventeenth year and reigns two years. He does evil, walking in the ways of his father, his mother, and Jeroboam, and serves and worships Baal.

l: The Second Book of Kings, The Second Book of Kings, The Second Book of Kings / Chapter 1
s: After Ahab's death, Moab rebelled against Israel. Ahaziah, injured in a fall through the lattice of his upper room in Samaria, sent messengers to ask Baal Zebub, the god of Ekron, whether he would recover. The LORD's angel sent Elijah the Tishbite to intercept them with a message that Ahaziah would die, and Elijah twice called down fire from the sky that consumed a captain and his fifty men sent to bring him to the king. A third captain begged for mercy, the angel told Elijah to go with him, and Elijah delivered the same message of death to Ahaziah in person. Ahaziah died as the LORD had said, and Jehoram began to reign in his place because he had no son.

l: Elijah, The Second Book of Kings, The Second Book of Kings / Chapter 1
s: Elijah is sent by the LORD's angel to intercept Ahaziah's messengers and tell them the king will die because he sought Baal Zebub. He is identified by the messengers' description of a hairy man in a leather belt. He calls down fire from the sky on two captains of fifty and their men, spares the third captain who begs, and goes with him to tell Ahaziah in person that he will die.

l: Ahaziah, The Second Book of Kings, The Second Book of Kings / Chapter 1
s: Ahaziah falls through the lattice in his upper room in Samaria and becomes sick, then sends messengers to inquire of Baal Zebub whether he will recover. He sends three captains with fifty men each to Elijah, and the first two companies are consumed by fire. Elijah tells him he will not leave his bed, and he dies according to the LORD's word, with Jehoram reigning in his place because he had no son.

l: LORD, The Second Book of Kings, The Second Book of Kings / Chapter 1
s: The LORD, through his angel, directs Elijah to confront the king's messengers, asking whether there is no God in Israel, and declares that Ahaziah will die. His angel later tells Elijah to go down with the third captain and not be afraid. The LORD's word spoken by Elijah is fulfilled when Ahaziah dies.

l: Baal Zebub, The Second Book of Kings, The Second Book of Kings / Chapter 1
s: Baal Zebub, the god of Ekron, is the one Ahaziah sends messengers to ask about his recovery. This is the reason the LORD pronounces death on the king, since it implies there is no God in Israel to inquire of.

l: Ahaziah's messengers, The Second Book of Kings, The Second Book of Kings / Chapter 1
s: Ahaziah's messengers are sent to inquire of Baal Zebub but are met by Elijah and told to return to the king with the LORD's message of death. They return and report to the king, describing the man who met them as hairy and wearing a leather belt, which leads Ahaziah to identify him as Elijah the Tishbite.

l: fire from the sky (Elijah's call), The Second Book of Kings, The Second Book of Kings / Chapter 1
s: Elijah calls fire down from the sky, on the condition that he is a man of God, and it consumes the first captain of fifty and his men. It does the same to a second captain and his fifty. The third captain refers to these events when he begs for his life and the lives of his fifty, and no fire falls on them.

l: Ahaziah's sickness, The Second Book of Kings, The Second Book of Kings / Chapter 1
s: Ahaziah's sickness results from his fall through the lattice in his upper room in Samaria and prompts him to inquire of Baal Zebub about recovery. The LORD declares through Elijah that he will not come down from his bed but will surely die, and the king dies of it as foretold.

l: The Second Book of Kings, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 2
s: Elijah, about to be taken up into heaven by a whirlwind, travels with Elisha from Gilgal to Bethel, Jericho, and the Jordan, and Elisha refuses three times to leave him despite warnings from the sons of the prophets. Elijah strikes the Jordan with his rolled-up mantle, the waters divide, and after Elisha asks for a double portion of his spirit, a chariot of fire and horses of fire separate them and Elijah goes up by a whirlwind. Elisha tears his clothes, takes up the fallen mantle, strikes the Jordan, and crosses over, and the sons of the prophets at Jericho recognize that Elijah's spirit rests on him. After fifty men search three days in vain for Elijah, Elisha heals Jericho's bad water by throwing salt into its spring at the LORD's word. On the way to Bethel, Elisha curses youths who mock him as 'baldy,' and two female bears maul forty-two of them before he continues to Mount Carmel and Samaria.

l: Elijah, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 2
s: Elijah travels with Elisha from Gilgal through Bethel and Jericho to the Jordan, telling him each time to wait while the LORD sends him on. He parts the Jordan by striking it with his rolled-up mantle, tells Elisha that seeing him taken will determine whether his request is granted, and is taken up into heaven by a whirlwind after a chariot and horses of fire separate them.

l: Elisha, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 2
s: Elisha refuses three times to leave Elijah, asks for a double portion of his spirit, and sees him taken up, crying 'My father, my father, the chariots of Israel and its horsemen!' and tearing his clothes. He takes up Elijah's mantle, parts the Jordan, is recognized by the prophets as having Elijah's spirit, heals Jericho's waters, curses the mocking youths, and returns via Mount Carmel to Samaria.

l: LORD, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 2
s: The LORD is the one who takes Elijah up by a whirlwind and who sends Elijah on to Bethel, Jericho, and the Jordan. Elisha invokes him as 'the God of Elijah' when striking the Jordan, the waters divide, and he speaks through Elisha to heal Jericho's waters. Elisha also curses the youths in his name.

l: Jericho, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 2
s: Jericho is a stopping point where the sons of the prophets warn Elisha that Elijah will be taken, and where Elisha later stays while the fifty men search in vain. Its men tell Elisha that the city's location is pleasant but its water is bad and the land barren, and Elisha heals the water.

l: Jordan, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 2
s: The Jordan is divided by Elijah's mantle-strike so he and Elisha cross on dry ground. After Elijah is taken, Elisha strikes it with the same mantle, invoking the LORD, the God of Elijah, and it divides again for him.

l: sons of the prophets, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 2
s: The sons of the prophets at Bethel and Jericho tell Elisha that the LORD will take his master away that day, and fifty of them watch from a distance at the Jordan. After seeing Elisha part the river they declare that Elijah's spirit rests on him and bow to him. They then urge him until he allows them to send fifty men to search for Elijah, who find nothing in three days.

l: mantle (Elijah's mantle), The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 2
s: Elijah rolls up his mantle and strikes the Jordan to divide it. It falls from him when he is taken up, and Elisha picks it up and uses it to strike the Jordan, which divides for him.

l: chariot of fire and horses of fire, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 2
s: A chariot of fire and horses of fire appear and separate Elijah from Elisha as they walk and talk. Elijah then goes up by a whirlwind into heaven.

l: spring of the waters (Jericho's spring), The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 2
s: Elisha goes out to the spring of Jericho's waters and throws salt from a new jar into it. He declares in the LORD's name that the waters are healed and will no longer bring death or barrenness.

l: youths of Bethel, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 2
s: Youths come out of the city as Elisha goes up to Bethel and mock him, repeatedly saying 'Go up, you baldy!' Elisha curses them in the LORD's name, and forty-two of them are mauled by bears.

l: two female bears, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 2
s: Two female bears come out of the woods after Elisha curses the mocking youths in the LORD's name. They maul forty-two of the youths.

l: healing of Jericho's waters, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 2
s: At the request of the city's men, Elisha has a new jar of salt brought and throws the salt into the spring, saying the LORD has healed the waters. The text says the waters remained healed to this day, according to Elisha's word.

l: double portion of Elijah's spirit, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 2
s: Elisha asks for a double portion of Elijah's spirit before Elijah is taken, and Elijah calls it a hard thing, granted only if Elisha sees him taken. Elisha sees him go, and afterward the Jordan parts for him and the sons of the prophets say Elijah's spirit rests on him.

l: The Second Book of Kings, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 3
s: Jehoram son of Ahab becomes king of Israel, doing evil though removing Baal's pillar, and holds to the sins of Jeroboam. When Mesha king of Moab, who had supplied Israel with lambs and wool, rebels after Ahab's death, Jehoram enlists Jehoshaphat of Judah and the king of Edom, and the three march seven days into a waterless wilderness. At Jehoshaphat's urging they consult Elisha, who rebukes Jehoram but, for Jehoshaphat's sake, prophesies that trenches dug in the valley will fill with water and that Moab will be delivered to them. Water comes at dawn, Moab mistakes it for blood and is routed, and Israel devastates the land and besieges Kir Hareseth. Mesha, failing to break through, offers his oldest son as a burnt offering on the wall, and great wrath against Israel causes them to withdraw.
