l: Jehoram, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 3
s: Jehoram son of Ahab began a twelve-year reign over Israel in Samaria, doing evil but removing the pillar of Baal and holding to the sins of Jeroboam. He mustered Israel against rebellious Moab, allied with Jehoshaphat and the king of Edom, and despaired when the army lacked water. Elisha rebuked him, yet the campaign succeeded until Israel departed from Moab after Mesha's sacrifice.

l: Jehoshaphat, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 3
s: Jehoshaphat king of Judah agreed to join Jehoram against Moab, saying his people and horses were as Jehoram's. He asked for a prophet of the LORD, and Elisha said he would not even look at Jehoram were it not for respect for Jehoshaphat's presence.

l: Elisha, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 3
s: Elisha son of Shaphat, who had poured water on Elijah's hands, was identified by a servant as available to inquire of the LORD. He rebuked Jehoram, called for a musician, and then prophesied that the valley would fill with water and that Moab would be delivered and its land devastated.

l: Mesha, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 3
s: Mesha king of Moab was a sheep breeder who had supplied Israel with one hundred thousand lambs and the wool of one hundred thousand rams. He rebelled after Ahab died, and when the battle went against him and his attempt to break through to the king of Edom failed, he offered his oldest son as a burnt offering on the wall.

l: LORD, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 3
s: The LORD, through Elisha, promised water without wind or rain, called it an easy thing, and promised to deliver the Moabites into the kings' hands. The water came as foretold, though Jehoram had earlier feared the LORD had called the kings together to give them to Moab.

l: Israel, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 3
s: Israel under Jehoram mustered for war against rebellious Moab and marched with Judah and Edom. After the water appeared, the Israelites struck the Moabites, destroyed cities, ruined land, stopped springs, felled trees, and besieged Kir Hareseth. Great wrath came against them after Mesha's sacrifice, and they returned to their own land.

l: Moab, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 3
s: Moab rebelled against Israel after Ahab's death and gathered all able-bodied men at the border when the kings approached. Mistaking the red-looking water for blood, they went to plunder and were routed, and their land was devastated, leaving only the stones of Kir Hareseth.

l: Edom, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 3
s: The king of Edom joined Israel and Judah in the expedition by the way of the wilderness of Edom. He went down with the other two kings to Elisha, the water came by way of Edom, and Mesha's attempt to break through to him failed.

l: Moabite rebellion against Israel (Moab's revolt), The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 3
s: After Ahab died, the king of Moab rebelled against Israel, ending the supply of lambs and wool he had provided. This revolt prompted Jehoram to muster Israel and call on Jehoshaphat.

l: campaign against Moab (three kings' expedition), The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 3
s: Israel, Judah, and Edom marched seven days by a circuitous route and ran out of water, then consulted Elisha. After the miraculous water, they routed Moab, ravaged the land, and besieged Kir Hareseth, but withdrew after Mesha's sacrifice brought great wrath against Israel.

l: water (miraculous water in the valley), The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 3
s: Elisha prophesied that the trench-filled valley would fill with water without wind or rain. The next morning, about the time of the sacrifice, water came by way of Edom and filled the country. The sun made it look red as blood to the Moabites, who were deceived into attacking.

l: Mesha's oldest son, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 3
s: Mesha's oldest son, who would have reigned in his father's place, was taken by Mesha and offered as a burnt offering on the wall.

l: burnt offering (child sacrifice on the wall), The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 3
s: Mesha offered his oldest son as a burnt offering on the wall of Kir Hareseth after failing to break through. Great wrath came against Israel, and they departed and returned to their land.

l: The Second Book of Kings, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 4
s: Chapter 4 recounts four episodes involving Elisha, the man of God. A prophet's widow, threatened by a creditor who would take her two sons as slaves, fills borrowed containers from her one pot of oil at Elisha's direction and sells the oil to pay her debt. A prominent woman of Shunem builds a room for Elisha, is promised a son by him, and bears the child; when the boy later dies, she rides to Elisha at Mount Carmel, and Elisha, after prayer and stretching himself on the child, restores him to life. At Gilgal during a famine, Elisha makes poisoned stew safe by adding meal. Finally, he feeds a hundred men with twenty loaves of first fruits bread, with some left over according to the LORD's word.

l: Elisha, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 4
s: Elisha tells the widow to borrow containers and fill them from her oil, and later promises the Shunammite woman a son. He prays to the LORD and stretches himself on her dead child until the boy revives. He also renders the poisoned stew harmless with meal and feeds a hundred men with twenty loaves, saying the LORD promised leftovers.

l: Gehazi, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 4
s: Gehazi, Elisha's servant, calls the Shunammite woman and relays Elisha's offer, then tells Elisha she has no son and her husband is old. He tries to thrust her away at Carmel, is sent with Elisha's staff to lay it on the dead child's face, and reports that the child has not awakened. He later calls the Shunammite again to take up her son, and questions how twenty loaves could feed a hundred men.

l: Shunammite woman, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 4
s: The prominent woman of Shunem persuades Elisha to eat at her home and suggests building him a room on the roof. After Elisha promises her a son, which she doubts, she bears him. When the boy dies she lays him on Elisha's bed, rides to Mount Carmel, seizes Elisha's feet, vows not to leave him, and finally bows and takes up her revived son.

l: widow of the prophet, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 4
s: The widow of one of the sons of the prophets cries out to Elisha because a creditor is coming to take her two children as slaves. Following Elisha's instructions, she fills borrowed containers with oil behind a closed door. Elisha then tells her to sell the oil, pay her debt, and live on the rest with her sons.

l: pot of oil (the widow's pot of oil), The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 4
s: The pot of oil is the only thing the widow has in her house. It supplies oil to fill all the borrowed containers until no more containers are available, and then the oil stops flowing.

l: sons of the prophets, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 4
s: The sons of the prophets are the group to which the widow's late husband belonged, and they sit before Elisha at Gilgal during a famine. They eat stew made with unrecognized wild gourds, cry out that there is death in the pot, and then eat safely after Elisha adds meal.

l: LORD, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 4
s: The LORD is the one the widow's husband feared and the one Elisha prays to for the dead child. He had hidden the Shunammite's trouble from Elisha. He also spoke the word that the hundred men would eat with leftovers, which came to pass.

l: son (the Shunammite's son), The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 4
s: The Shunammite's son is born at the season Elisha foretold. When grown, he cries "My head!" in the field with the reapers, is carried to his mother, sits on her knees until noon and dies. After Elisha's prayer and stretching himself on him, the boy's flesh grows warm, he sneezes seven times, and opens his eyes.

l: stew pot (Elisha's large pot), The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 4
s: Elisha has his servant set the large pot on to boil stew for the sons of the prophets. Wild gourds cut into it make the men cry out that there is death in the pot, but after Elisha throws in meal there is nothing harmful in it.

l: first fruits bread, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 4
s: A man from Baal Shalishah brings Elisha twenty loaves of barley and fresh ears of grain as first fruits bread. Elisha orders it given to the people, and it feeds a hundred men with some left over, as the LORD said.

l: resurrection of the Shunammite's son, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 4
s: After Gehazi's staff fails to wake the dead child, Elisha shuts the door, prays to the LORD, and stretches himself on the boy twice. The child warms, sneezes seven times, and opens his eyes, and Elisha tells the Shunammite to take up her son.

l: The Second Book of Kings, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 5
s: Naaman, the Syrian army captain who is a leper, learns from a captive Israelite girl that a prophet in Samaria could heal him, and the king of Syria sends him to the king of Israel with a letter and gifts. The king of Israel tears his clothes in alarm, but Elisha tells Naaman to wash seven times in the Jordan. Naaman is first enraged but, persuaded by his servants, obeys and is healed, then confesses that there is no God but in Israel and offers Elisha a gift, which Elisha refuses. Elisha's servant Gehazi secretly runs after Naaman, lies to obtain silver and clothing, and then lies to Elisha about it. Elisha rebukes him and declares that Naaman's leprosy will cling to Gehazi and his offspring forever, and Gehazi leaves leprous, white as snow.

l: Naaman, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 5
s: Naaman, captain of the Syrian army, is a great and valiant man but a leper, and he travels to Israel at his king's direction seeking healing. He is angered when Elisha only sends a messenger telling him to wash in the Jordan, but his servants persuade him, and he dips seven times and is made clean. He declares that there is no God in all the earth but in Israel, offers a gift that is refused, asks for two mules' load of earth, vows to offer sacrifice only to the LORD, and asks pardon for bowing in the house of Rimmon when accompanying his master.

l: Elisha, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 5
s: Elisha, the man of God in Samaria, tells the king of Israel to send Naaman to him and sends a messenger instructing Naaman to wash in the Jordan seven times. He refuses Naaman's gift, swearing by the LORD, and tells Naaman to go in peace. He perceives Gehazi's deceit, rebukes him, and pronounces that Naaman's leprosy will cling to Gehazi and his offspring forever.

l: Gehazi, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 5
s: Gehazi, Elisha's servant, resolves to take something from Naaman after his master refused a gift, and runs after him. He falsely claims that Elisha sent him to ask for a talent of silver and two changes of clothing for two young prophets, receives two talents and two changes of clothing, and hides them in the house. He lies to Elisha, saying he went nowhere, is rebuked, and leaves Elisha's presence a leper, white as snow.

l: king of Syria, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 5
s: The king of Syria honors Naaman, whose leadership brought Syria victory. On hearing about the prophet in Samaria, he sends Naaman with a letter to the king of Israel and ten talents of silver, six thousand pieces of gold, and ten changes of clothing, asking that Naaman be healed.

l: king of Israel, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 5
s: The king of Israel reads the Syrian king's letter and tears his clothes, asking whether he is God to kill and make alive, and suspecting that Syria seeks a quarrel with him. Elisha then sends word asking why he tore his clothes and telling him to let Naaman come to him.

l: little girl (Naaman's wife's servant), The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 5
s: The little girl, taken captive from Israel by Syrian bands, waits on Naaman's wife. She says she wishes her lord were with the prophet in Samaria, who would heal him of his leprosy, and her words are reported to the king and set the events in motion.

l: Israel, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 5
s: Israel is the land from which the Syrians took the little girl captive and where a prophet is said to be able to heal Naaman. Elisha says the healing will show that there is a prophet in Israel, and Naaman concludes that there is no God in all the earth but in Israel.

l: Jordan, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 5
s: The Jordan is the river in which Elisha instructs Naaman to wash seven times. Naaman at first scorns Israel's waters in favor of Abanah and Pharpar, the rivers of Damascus, but then dips himself seven times in the Jordan and is cleansed, his flesh restored like a little child's.

l: LORD, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 5
s: The LORD is credited with giving victory to Syria through Naaman, and Elisha swears by the LORD as living and as the one before whom he stands. Naaman, after his healing, vows to offer sacrifice only to the LORD and asks the LORD's pardon for bowing in the house of Rimmon. Gehazi also swears by the LORD while planning his deception.

l: leprosy, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 5
s: Leprosy afflicts Naaman despite his greatness, and he is healed of it after dipping seven times in the Jordan. It is then transferred to Gehazi as punishment for his greed and lying, with Elisha declaring that it will cling to him and his offspring forever.

l: gift to Elisha (Naaman's offering), The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 5
s: After being healed, Naaman urges Elisha to accept a gift from him. Elisha swears by the LORD that he will receive none and refuses even when pressed.

l: talents of silver and clothing (Gehazi's request), The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 5
s: Gehazi falsely asks Naaman for a talent of silver and two changes of clothing in Elisha's name for two supposed visitors. Naaman presses two talents of silver in two bags and two changes of clothing on him, and servants carry them until Gehazi takes them and stores them in his house. Elisha's rebuke over this wealth leads to Gehazi's affliction with leprosy.

l: The Second Book of Kings, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 6
s: Elisha helps the sons of the prophets build a new dwelling by the Jordan, making a borrowed ax head float after it falls into the water. The king of Syria, at war with Israel, finds his plans repeatedly revealed to the king of Israel by Elisha, and sends an army to surround Elisha in Dothan. Elisha's servant sees the hosts of fire protecting them, the Syrians are struck blind and led to Samaria, and Elisha has them fed rather than killed, so the Syrian raids stop. Later Benhadad besieges Samaria, causing a terrible famine in which two women have eaten one woman's son, and the king of Israel, hearing this, vows to behead Elisha. Elisha foresees the messenger's coming, and the king's messenger arrives declaring that this evil is from the LORD.

l: Elisha, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 6
s: Elisha goes with the sons of the prophets to the Jordan and makes a lost borrowed ax head float with a cut stick. He reveals the Syrian king's plans to the king of Israel, prays that his servant's eyes be opened and that the Syrian army be blinded, then leads them to Samaria and tells the king of Israel to feed them rather than strike them. When the king vows to take his head, Elisha, sitting with the elders, foresees the messenger and tells them to hold the door shut.

l: king of Syria, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 6
s: The king of Syria wages war on Israel, but his camp plans are repeatedly thwarted because Elisha tells the king of Israel. Troubled, he learns from a servant that Elisha reveals even his bedroom words, and sends horses, chariots, and a great army to seize Elisha at Dothan. The text then names Benhadad king of Syria, who gathers his whole army and besieges Samaria.

l: Syrians, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 6
s: The Syrians are warned of by Elisha as coming down to a certain place, allowing Israel's king to avoid them. After they are fed in Samaria, the Syrian bands stop raiding Israel's land, though Benhadad later besieges Samaria.

l: Jehoram, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 6
s: The king of Israel heeds Elisha's warnings and saves himself more than once. When the blinded Syrians are brought to Samaria he asks Elisha whether to strike them, and obeys by feeding them a great feast and sending them home. During the siege he hears the woman's complaint, tears his clothes to reveal sackcloth beneath, and vows Elisha's head will not stay on him that day.

l: Israel, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 6
s: Israel is attacked by Syria and is protected through Elisha's warnings. Its land is spared further Syrian raids after the Syrians are fed, but later Samaria is besieged and suffers severe famine.

l: Syrian army (sent against Elisha), The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 6
s: A great army of horses and chariots comes by night and surrounds Dothan to seize Elisha. Elisha prays and they are struck blind, he leads them to Samaria, and their eyes are opened to find themselves in the middle of the city. They are fed and sent back to their master unharmed.

l: servant of Elisha, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 6
s: Elisha's servant rises early, sees the army around Dothan, and cries out in fear to Elisha. Elisha prays, and the LORD opens the young man's eyes so he sees the mountain full of horses and chariots of fire around Elisha.

l: LORD, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 6
s: The LORD opens the eyes of Elisha's servant to see the fiery host, strikes the Syrians with blindness at Elisha's prayer, and opens their eyes again in Samaria. The king of Israel invokes him when speaking to the woman, and the messenger says this evil is from the LORD.

l: horses and chariots of fire, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 6
s: Horses and chariots of fire fill the mountain around Elisha when the LORD opens his servant's eyes. They show that those with Elisha are more than those with the Syrians.

l: Samaria, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 6
s: Elisha leads the blinded Syrian army into Samaria, where their eyes are opened in the middle of the city and they are fed. Later Benhadad besieges Samaria, and it suffers a great famine.

l: siege of Samaria, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 6
s: After the earlier episode, Benhadad king of Syria gathers all his army and besieges Samaria. The siege causes extreme famine and leads to the woman's appeal to the king on the wall.

l: famine in Samaria, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 6
s: The famine becomes so severe that a donkey's head sells for eighty pieces of silver and a fourth of a kab of dove's dung for five. It drives two women to boil and eat a son, and the king tears his clothes when he hears of it.

l: woman who appealed to the king, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 6
s: She cries out to the king of Israel on the wall for help. She tells him that she and another woman agreed to eat her son one day and the other's son the next, but after they ate hers the other woman hid her son.

l: sons of the two women, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 6
s: The first woman's son is boiled and eaten during the famine, as agreed with the other woman. The other woman's son is hidden by his mother rather than given up to be eaten.

l: The Second Book of Kings, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 7
s: Elisha announces that within a day flour and barley will sell cheaply in the gate of Samaria, and the captain on whose hand the king leans scoffs and is told he will see it but not eat of it. Four leprous men, deciding to surrender to the Syrians rather than die, find the Syrian camp deserted because the Lord made the Syrians hear a great army and flee. After eating and taking goods, the lepers tell the city gatekeepers, and the king, suspecting a trap, sends riders who confirm the Syrians' flight along the path to the Jordan. The people plunder the camp, prices fall as Elisha said, and the captain is trampled to death in the gate.

l: Elisha, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 7
s: Elisha, called the man of God, announces the Lord's word that a seah of fine flour and two seahs of barley will each sell for a shekel in the gate of Samaria by the same time the next day. He also tells the doubting captain that he will see it but not eat of it, and both statements come true.

l: LORD, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 7
s: The Lord caused the Syrian army to hear the sound of chariots, horses, and a great army, so that they fled in the twilight. His word through Elisha about the cheap flour and barley is fulfilled, and so is the word about the captain's death.

l: captain (on whose hand the king leaned), The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 7
s: The captain scoffs at Elisha's prophecy, asking whether it could happen even if the Lord made windows in heaven. The king appoints him to be in charge of the gate, where the people trample him and he dies, as the man of God had said.

l: king of Israel, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 7
s: The king rises in the night after hearing the lepers' report and suspects the Syrians are hiding in the field to ambush the starving city. He follows a servant's advice to send two chariots with horses to look, and they return confirming the Syrians' flight. He had appointed the captain to be in charge of the gate.

l: four leprous men, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 7
s: Four leprous men at the gate, reasoning that they will die whether they stay or enter the famished city, go to surrender to the Syrians and find the camp empty. They eat, drink, and hide silver, gold, and clothing from two tents, then, judging that they are not doing right, tell the gatekeepers so the king's household learns the news.

l: Syrians, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 7
s: The Syrians, having heard a sound of chariots and horses that the Lord caused, believed the king of Israel had hired the Hittite and Egyptian kings against them. They fled in the twilight, leaving tents, horses, donkeys, and the camp as it was, and scattering garments and equipment along the path to the Jordan.

l: Samaria, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 7
s: Samaria is the place where the gate will see flour and barley sold for a shekel, according to Elisha's word. The people there are in famine, and the prophecy is fulfilled after the Syrian camp is plundered.
